title: Generics Fundamentals and Type Parameters
learningObjectives: Declare generic classes with reusable type parameters such as T
Use parameterized collections to preserve compile-time type safety
Create generic objects with inferred or explicit type arguments
Avoid raw collection types and unnecessary unchecked casts
Explain why wrapper classes represent primitive values in generics

understand.concept: Generics let classes and methods work with types while preserving compile-time checks. Parameterized collections avoid unsafe casts.
understand.whyItMatters: Generics Fundamentals and Type Parameters helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Why Java has generics

Generics let a class, interface or method work with a type selected by its caller while retaining compile-time type checking. A declaration such as List<String> communicates that the list is intended to contain String values. Reading an element returns String without a manual cast, and adding an incompatible type is rejected by the compiler.

## Type parameters and arguments

A type parameter is a placeholder declared by a generic type, commonly named T, E, K or V. A type argument is the concrete type supplied when the generic type is used. For example, Box<T> declares a type parameter, while Box<String> supplies String as its type argument.

## Build a generic class

A generic class declares its type parameters after the class name. Its fields and methods can use those parameters. The same class can then hold different reference types without duplicating the implementation. The compiler checks that values read and written through the generic API agree with the selected type.

## Parameterized collections and raw types

Prefer List<String> over raw List. Raw types bypass much of the compiler's generic checking and can introduce heap pollution or ClassCastException later. Avoid unchecked casts when a parameterized declaration expresses the required type directly.

## Primitive types and wrappers

Java type arguments must be reference types, not primitive types. Use wrapper classes such as Integer, Double and Boolean with generic collections. Autoboxing converts between a primitive value and its wrapper where the language permits it; unboxing a null wrapper causes NullPointerException.

## Type erasure

Java implements generics using type erasure for most runtime representation. Generic type information is primarily enforced by the compiler, and ordinary code cannot test an object with expressions such as value instanceof T. Arrays of a non-reifiable parameterized type cannot be created directly. Understand these limits when designing generic APIs.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.List<String> names = new java.util.ArrayList<>(); names.add("Asha"); System.out.println(names.get(0)); } }
examples.explanation: The parameterized List<String> declaration constrains inserted values to String and allows retrieval without an explicit cast.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { class Box<T> { private final T value; Box(T value) { this.value=value; } T get() { return value; } } Box<Integer> box = new Box<>(7); System.out.println(box.get()); } }
examples.explanation: Box<T> declares a reusable type parameter; constructing Box<String> fixes T as String for this object.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.List<Integer> values = java.util.List.of(1,2,3); System.out.println(values.get(2) + 1); } }
examples.explanation: List<Integer> returns Integer values, so the program can assign a retrieved element to an Integer without a cast.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<String,Integer> scores = java.util.Map.of("Asha",90); System.out.println(scores.get("Asha")); } }
examples.explanation: Map<String, Integer> declares separate type parameters for keys and values; the compiler checks both positions.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("Parameterized types are checked at compile time"); } }
examples.expectedOutput: Parameterized types are checked at compile time
examples.explanation: The diamond operator lets the compiler infer the constructor's type arguments from the declared variable type.

practise.guidedTask: Create a generic Box<T> class and use it with String and Integer. Show how the compiler rejects assigning the wrong type.
practise.independentTask: Refactor a raw List into List<String>, remove unnecessary casts and demonstrate a compile-time type mismatch.
hints: Read the generic declaration to identify its type parameters, then read the use site to identify the supplied type arguments.
Use wrapper classes such as Integer rather than int in generic type arguments.
Prefer parameterized types over raw collections so invalid values are rejected at compile time.
practise.challenge: Create a generic Pair<K,V> class and use it for a product code and price; explain why primitive types need wrapper classes.

questions.prompt: What does a generic type parameter such as T represent?
options: A type supplied when the generic class or method is used
A runtime variable containing source code
questions.answer: A type supplied when the generic class or method is used
questions.explanation: List<String> fixes the element type to String at compile time, allowing retrieval without a cast and rejecting other element types.

questions.prompt: Which declaration uses a parameterized collection safely?
questions.explanation: The class declares a type parameter T; Box<Integer> supplies Integer, so get returns an Integer value.

questions.prompt: What is a benefit of generics?
options: Compile-time type checking and fewer unsafe casts
questions.answer: Compile-time type checking and fewer unsafe casts
questions.explanation: The third element is Integer 3; adding 1 produces 4 through unboxing and numeric addition.

questions.prompt: Why are raw collection types discouraged?
options: They bypass generic type checks and can cause unsafe casts
questions.answer: They bypass generic type checks and can cause unsafe casts
questions.explanation: Map declares two type arguments: String for keys and Integer for values, so get returns the mapped score.

questions.prompt: Can Java generics use primitive types directly as type arguments?
options: No; use wrapper types such as Integer
questions.answer: No; use wrapper types such as Integer
questions.explanation: The diamond operator lets the compiler infer constructor type arguments from the target context, avoiding repeated generic type notation.
